# Old helper names for streams give no warning

## What happens now
Right now the two helpers that give a program a stream for reading and writing live in the click.utils module under the plain names get_binary_stream and get_text_stream. They look like normal, everyday names, and the same plain names are also shown straight from the main click module. When someone reaches for either of these names, nothing tells them the name is old and is going away in Click 9.0. Some of the other old names in click.utils do warn, but these two stay silent.

## What should happen
When someone reaches for the old get_binary_stream or get_text_stream name, either from the main click module or from the click.utils module, that person should see a clear message saying the name is old and will be removed in Click 9.0.

## About this project
This project is a toolkit for building command line programs in Python. It helps people handle arguments, options, prompts, output, and files, so they can focus on what their program does. Many people build their own tools on top of it, so the names it offers them matter.

## Problem this solves
People cannot tell that these two helper names are on their way out, so their scripts keep using names that will one day disappear. A clear message lets them move to the current names before that happens.

## What changed
The two helpers now have names that start with an underscore, so they no longer look like everyday names. The part of click.utils that answers for old names now also answers for get_binary_stream and get_text_stream and gives the same kind of old-name message. The wording used for the other old names in that same place now matches this wording. The documentation sentence about closing files that are opened only when used is reworded.

## Impact
Ease of use and a clearer path when upgrading.

## User experience
Before: a person writes a small program and reaches for the old get_binary_stream name from click; the program runs with no message at all, so the person has no idea the name is old. After: the same person uses that old name and sees a message saying it is old and will be removed in Click 9.0, so they know to switch to the current name.

   7 │ different decoding of parameters.
   8 │ 
   9 │ Here is a brief overview of how this works and what it means to you.
  10 │ 
  11 │ ## Unicode Arguments
  12 │ 
  13 │ Click internally is generally based on the concept that any argument can come in as either byte string or unicode string
  14 │ and conversion is performed to the type expected value as late as possible. This has some advantages as it allows us to
  15 │ accept the data in the most appropriate form for the operating system and Python version.
  16 │ 
  17 │ This caused some problems on Windows where initially the wrong encoding was used and garbage ended up in your input
  18 │ data. We not only fixed the encoding part, but we also now extract unicode parameters from `sys.argv`.
  19 │ 
  20 │ There is also another limitation with this: if `sys.argv` was modified prior to invoking a click handler, we have to
  21 │ fall back to the regular byte input in which case not all unicode values are available but only a subset of the codepage
  22 │ used for parameters.
  23 │ 
  24 │ ## Unicode Output and Input
  25 │ 
  26 │ Unicode output and input on Windows is implemented through the concept of a
  27 │ dispatching text stream. This means that when click first needs a text output
  28 │ (or input) stream on windows it goes through a few checks to figure out if a
  29 │ windows console is connected or not. If no Windows console is present then the
  30 │ text output stream is returned as such and the encoding for that stream is set
  31 │ to `utf-8` like on all platforms.
  32 │ 
  33 │ However if a console is connected the stream will instead be emulated and use the cmd.exe unicode APIs to output text
  34 │ information. In this case the stream will also use `utf-16-le` as internal encoding. However there is some hackery going
  35 │ on that the underlying raw IO buffer is still bypassing the unicode APIs and byte output through an indirection is still
  36 │ possible.
  37 │ 
  38 │ - This unicode support is limited to `click.echo`, `click.prompt` as well as `click.get_text_stream`.
  39 │ - Depending on if unicode values or byte strings are passed the control flow goes completely different places internally
  40 │   which can have some odd artifacts if data partially ends up being buffered. Click attempts to protect against that by
  41 │   manually always flushing but if you are mixing and matching different string types to `stdout` or `stderr` you will
  42 │   need to manually flush.
  43 │ - The raw output stream is set to binary mode, which is a global operation on Windows, so `print` calls will be
  44 │   affected. Prefer `click.echo` over `print`.
  45 │ - On Windows 7 and below, there is a limitation where at most 64k characters can be written in one call in binary mode.
  46 │   In this situation, `sys.stdout` and `sys.stderr` are replaced with wrappers that work around the limitation.
  47 │ 
  48 │ Another important thing to note is that the Windows console's default fonts do not support a lot of characters which
  49 │ means that you are mostly limited to international letters but no emojis or special characters.

   3 │ # Handling Files
   4 │ 
   5 │ ```{currentmodule} click
   6 │ ```
   7 │ 
   8 │ Click has built in features to support file and file path handling. The examples use arguments but the same principle
   9 │ applies to options as well.
  10 │ 
  11 │ (file-args)=
  12 │ 
  13 │ ## File Arguments
  14 │ 
  15 │ Click supports working with files with the {class}`File` type. Some notable features are:
  16 │ 
  17 │ - Support for `-` to mean a special file that refers to stdin when used for reading, and stdout when used for writing.
  18 │   This is a common pattern for POSIX command line utilities.
  19 │ - Deals with `str` and `bytes` correctly for all versions of Python.
  20 │ 
  21 │ Example:
  22 │ 
  23 │ ```{eval-rst}
  24 │ .. click:example::
  25 │ 
  26 │     @click.command()
  27 │     @click.argument('input', type=click.File('rb'))
  28 │     @click.argument('output', type=click.File('wb'))
  29 │     def inout(input, output):
  30 │         """Copy contents of INPUT to OUTPUT."""
  31 │         while True:
  32 │             chunk = input.read(1024)
  33 │             if not chunk:
  34 │                 break
  35 │             output.write(chunk)
  36 │ 
  37 │ And from the command line:
  38 │ 
  39 │ .. click:run::
  40 │ 
  41 │     with isolated_filesystem():
  42 │         invoke(inout, args=['-', 'hello.txt'], input=['hello'],
  43 │                terminate_input=True)
  44 │         invoke(inout, args=['hello.txt', '-'])
  45 │ ```
  46 │ 
  47 │ ## File Path Arguments
  48 │ 
  49 │ For handling paths, the {class}`Path` type is better than a `str`. Some notable features are:
  50 │ 
  51 │ - The `exists` argument will verify whether the path exists.
  52 │ - `readable`, `writable`, and `executable` can perform permission checks.
  53 │ - `file_okay` and `dir_okay` allow specifying whether files/directories are accepted.
  54 │ - Error messages are nicely formatted using {func}`format_filename` so any undecodable bytes will be printed nicely.
  55 │ 
  56 │ See {class}`Path` for all features.
  57 │ 
  58 │ Example:
  59 │ 
  60 │ ```{eval-rst}
  61 │ .. click:example::
  62 │ 
  63 │     @click.command()
  64 │     @click.argument('filename', type=click.Path(exists=True))
  65 │     def touch(filename):
  66 │         """Print FILENAME if the file exists."""
  67 │         click.echo(click.format_filename(filename))
  68 │ 
  69 │ And from the command line:
  70 │ 
  71 │ .. click:run::
  72 │ 
  73 │     with isolated_filesystem():
  74 │         with open('hello.txt', 'w') as f:
  75 │             f.write('Hello World!\n')
  76 │         invoke(touch, args=['hello.txt'])
  77 │         println()
  78 │         invoke(touch, args=['missing.txt'])
  79 │ ```
  80 │ 
  81 │ ## File Opening Behaviors
  82 │ 
  83 │ The {class}`File` type attempts to be "intelligent" about when to open a file. Stdin/stdout and files opened for reading
  84 │ will be opened immediately. This will give the user direct feedback when a file cannot be opened. Files opened for
  85 │ writing will only be open on the first IO operation. This is done by automatically wrapping the file in a special
  86 │ wrapper.
  87 │ 
  88 │ File open behavior can be controlled by the boolean kwarg `lazy`. If a file is opened lazily:
  89 │ 
  90 │ - A failure at first IO operation will happen by raising an {exc}`FileError`.
  91 │ - It can help minimize resource handling confusion. If a file is opened in lazy mode, it will call
  92 │   {meth}`_LazyFile.close_intelligently` to help figure out if the file needs closing or not. This is not needed for
  93 │   parameters, but is necessary for manually prompting. For manual prompts with the {func}`prompt` function you do not
  94 │   know if a stream like stdout was opened (which was already open before) or a real file was opened (that needs
  95 │   closing).
  96 │ 
  97 │ Since files opened for writing will typically empty the file, the lazy mode should only be disabled if the developer is
  98 │ absolutely sure that this is intended behavior.
  99 │ 
 100 │ It is also possible to open files in atomic mode by passing `atomic=True`. In atomic mode, all writes go into a separate
 101 │ file in the same folder, and upon completion, the file will be moved over to the original location. This is useful if a
 102 │ file regularly read by other users is modified.
